claims.text: A framework combining high-throughput DSC and dilatometry with reduced-order machine-learning models informed by DFT and CALPHAD can accurately and efficiently predict melting and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across multi-principal-element high-entropy alloys.
The target materials are solid-solution HEAs containing 4–8 principal components in nominally equimolar or near-equimolar ratios.
Iteratively feeding targeted measurements into an active-learning model will reduce predictive uncertainty across HEA composition space.
Finite-temperature first-principles and CALPHAD calculations can provide physically informed initial predictions for HEA phase and thermodynamic behavior.
Real-time DSC under controlled inert or vacuum heating measures the heat-flow behavior through the melting interval.
Dilatometry can track the volume change of HEAs during melting.
High configurational entropy influences phase stability and liquid-phase structural configurations in multi-component HEAs.
Phase stability and liquid-phase structural configurations govern melting and fusion thermodynamics.
Combining physically informed calculations with uncertainty-driven sampling allows the model to learn structure–property correlations and refine predictions as new data are acquired.
For newly sampled HEAs, melting temperature will be predicted within ±10 K.
For newly sampled HEAs, enthalpy and entropy of fusion will each be predicted within ±5%.
For newly sampled HEAs, volume change on melting will be predicted within ±5%.
Key liquid-phase properties will be predicted within approximately 10% of measured values.
The adaptive framework will outperform standalone high-throughput experiments and non-iterative computation–experiment pipelines.
Independent DFT or CALPHAD predictions and one-shot experimental approaches can have large uncertainty for compositionally complex alloys.
The approach depends on representative initial data and valid thermodynamic databases for the relevant elements and alloy systems.
Complex intermetallics and temperatures outside the training range may degrade model performance unless additional experiments expand coverage.
Generalization to alloy systems with minimal prior data is unverified and may fail when training data do not cover the relevant chemistry or phase space.

Prospective validation on multiple untested, compositionally diverse HEAs can evaluate model generalization by comparing predictions with DSC, dilatometry, density, and in situ diffraction measurements.
Deviation greater than 20% for multiple prospective compositions is specified as the rejection criterion for the workflow.
